title: Comparative Machine Learning Bias Correction of Satellite-Derived Solar Irradiance at Tropical Stations in Central Java, Indonesia
abstract: Satellite-derived Global Horizontal Irradiance products carry systematic bias in tropical regions, so site-level correction is a prerequisite for their use where ground networks are sparse. This study compares bias-correction methods for NASA POWER daily irradiance in Central Java, Indonesia, and asks how much reported accuracy reflects algebraic dependence between predictors and the ground reference. Ten PUSDATARU stations were analysed over 2020–2024 (17,072 station-days; 8,459 from five exactly co-located stations). Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, Elastic Net, and Quantile Mapping were trained chronologically (2020–2022/2023/2024) against persistence and climatology baselines, with preprocessing fitted on training data only, paired significance tests, leave-one-station-out validation, and SHAP attribution. Random Forest reduced RMSE from 3.398 to 2.674 MJ m⁻² day⁻¹ (21.3%), lowered mean bias from 0.988 to 0.221, and raised R² from 0.266 to 0.546; across ten stations XGBoost reduced error from 5.921 to 2.831. Differences among tree ensembles were not statistically robust, and the weighted ensemble gave no gain at the highest inference cost. Adding ground-observed sunshine as a predictor raised the coefficient of determination to 0.9994, identified as recovery of the Ångström–Prescott expression defining the reference (70.9% attribution). Near-perfect accuracies against sunshine-derived references therefore measure leakage, not skill; correction also failed to transfer spatially, motivating sub-degree geostationary products as the next step.

title: Seeing the Options: What Should a Visual Candidate See?
abstract: Agents often choose among candidates that are images: elements of a screenshot, product photos, charts. A single-pass decision model either encodes the request and all candidates as one sequence, making its answer depend on candidate order, or encodes each candidate alone, which keeps order invariance and reusable encodings but hides the request from the candidate. We ask where the joint encoder's advantage comes from: from candidates seeing the request, or from candidates seeing each other while they are encoded. With one backbone and the same fine-tuning steps on screenshot crops of Multimodal-Mind2Web, the answer is mostly the request. Continuing each candidate from a forked cache of the encoded request recovers 11 to 13 of the 12 to 17 points that independent encoding loses to joint encoding, at the price of cross-request reuse, and we prove that order invariance stays exact whenever candidates never see each other. A joint encoder retrained with its candidates isolated from one another during encoding loses 1.1 and 0.4 ranking points in one paired run (0.7 and 0.3 against the mean of five joint runs), and permutation-equivariant interactions among candidates, over pooled vectors or inside the encoder, gain nothing beyond continued training. At a matched abstention operating point the state-conditioned model is 0.6 and 1.0 points below the joint encoder (mean of four runs) with a flip rate of zero, against 8-10% for the joint encoder; on AndroidControl crops (three and five runs) it is 2.5 to 4 ranking points below. Finally, the abstention threshold drifts: the choice term of the loss ignores the score level, and the coverage term pins it only weakly once positives saturate; a quantile threshold aligns operating points.

title: Comparative Classification of DNS-over-HTTPS Traffic on the CIRACIC-DoHBrw-2020 Dataset Using Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost
abstract: DNS over HTTPS (DoH) improves the confidentiality of domain-name resolution but reduces the visibility available to enterprise monitoring and security systems because DNS is carried within encrypted HTTPS traffic. This study compares Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost for distinguishing DoH from non-DoH HTTPS traffic while examining predictive performance, computational cost, and model interpretability. The models were evaluated using the cleaned Layer 1 representation of the CIRA-CIC-DoHBrw-2020 dataset, which contains 1,019,117 flow records and 29 statistical predictors. The controlled protocol used three repeated 80:20 stratified development-test splits (seeds 42, 52, and 62), three-fold cross-validation, class-imbalance treatment, held-out testing, execution-time measurement, and permutation importance. Random Forest produced the strongest threshold-dependent results, achieving a macro F1 of 0.9965, MCC of 0.9930, and false-positive rate of 0.0011. XGBoost obtained the highest Average Precision (0.9994) and required a mean training time of 31.40 seconds, approximately 95.8% lower than Random Forest (743.42 seconds). Logistic Regression was computationally efficient but yielded lower DoH precision and a false-positive rate of 0.1197. PacketLengthMode was the most influential feature for both tree-based models. The results demonstrate strong within-benchmark separation, but they do not establish cross-network or operational generalisation.

title: Gender Associations in LLM-Mediated ADHD Self-Diagnosis
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for medical self-diagnosis. However, the way demographic cues shape outputs in these interactions remains poorly understood. This is particularly consequential for diagnoses like ADHD, where persistent gender disparities are not fully aligned with the clinical evidence. We adapt the Context Association Test (CAT) to evaluate whether GPT-4o responds to gendered ADHD associations in a zero-shot, self-diagnostic setting. We show that explicit cueing consistently amplifies certain ADHD subtype associations while implicit cueing produces near proxy-aligned distributions. These divergences suggest that explicit demographic cues may activate bias-mitigation mechanisms that over-correct rather than eliminate bias, whereas implicit cues appear to reflect the model's default behavior. Our results demonstrate that evaluating gendered bias in LLM-mediated self-diagnosis requires careful attention to the demographic associations a model encodes.

title: The Future Is Finer: Multivariate Time Series Super-Resolution Forecasting
abstract: Web platforms run on multivariate time series, from service telemetry and Web traffic logs to sensor streams served through Web APIs. Yet, retention policies often archive them at coarse granularity to save storage and bandwidth. Decisions such as autoscaling, alerting, and billing operate at finer granularity than existing forecasters reach, since these models predict at the resolution of their input. We therefore introduce Multivariate Time Series Super-Resolution Forecasting (MTS-SRF), which forecasts fine-grained futures from coarse histories, and propose TimeMagnifier to address its three challenges. Fourier Anchor counters data sparsity by fitting each input window to a trend-Fourier structure with sparse cross-variable gating; De-noise Only constrains fine-grained ambiguity by refining along the resolution axis rather than the noise axis, lengthening the grid level by level; and banded DTW Alignment corrects cross-resolution misalignment against the coarse forecast. On the first MTS-SRF benchmark, with ten datasets from five domains, real archived cross-resolution pairs, strengthened baseline adaptations, and five-seed significance tests, TimeMagnifier is best on every dataset, resolution coefficient, and metric against 15 baselines and cuts MSE by 12.3% on average. Its De-noise Only and DTW stages also transfer as a plug-in that lowers the MSE of existing forecasters by 5.1% to 9.0%. Code will be made publicly available.

evidence.title: The Future Is Finer: Multivariate Time Series Super-Resolution Forecasting
evidence.abstract: Web platforms run on multivariate time series, from service telemetry and Web traffic logs to sensor streams served through Web APIs. Yet, retention policies often archive them at coarse granularity to save storage and bandwidth. Decisions such as autoscaling, alerting, and billing operate at finer granularity than existing forecasters reach, since these models predict at the resolution of their input. We therefore introduce Multivariate Time Series Super-Resolution Forecasting (MTS-SRF), which forecasts fine-grained futures from coarse histories, and propose TimeMagnifier to address its three challenges. Fourier Anchor counters data sparsity by fitting each input window to a trend-Fourier structure with sparse cross-variable gating; De-noise Only constrains fine-grained ambiguity by refining along the resolution axis rather than the noise axis, lengthening the grid level by level; and banded DTW Alignment corrects cross-resolution misalignment against the coarse forecast. On the first MTS-SRF benchmark, with ten datasets from five domains, real archived cross-resolution pairs, strengthened baseline adaptations, and five-seed significance tests, TimeMagnifier is best on every dataset, resolution coefficient, and metric against 15 baselines and cuts MSE by 12.3% on average. Its De-noise Only and DTW stages also transfer as a plug-in that lowers the MSE of existing forecasters by 5.1% to 9.0%. Code will be made publicly available.

title: Scalable Unrolled Chains for MRI Reconstruction
abstract: Unrolled variational networks achieve state-of-the-art performance for accelerated MRI reconstruction, but standard end-to-end training becomes prohibitively memory intensive as the number and width of cascades increase. We propose a memory-efficient training framework that updates a randomly sampled cascade while retaining supervision from the final reconstruction loss. The error signal is propagated from the end of the chain to the sampled cascade using an activation-light backward pass that avoids storing full chain activations, thereby decoupling training memory from chain length. A time-conditioned network shared across cascades further keeps the parameter count independent of chain length. The backward pass is approximate only through frozen normalization statistics, and a trained exact gradient control shows the approximation leaves reconstruction quality unchanged. The framework remains trainable at chain lengths and cascade widths where standard end-to-end backpropagation exhausts GPU memory. On fastMRI single-coil knee and multi-coil brain reconstruction, our method consistently outperforms other local training approaches. On high-SNR knee slices, our method surpasses E2E-VarNet at $8\times$ and matches it at $4\times$, while on the complete brain validation set it surpasses E2E-VarNet at $8\times$ and achieves comparable performance at $4\times$, with fewer parameters, lower peak memory, and faster per-iteration training. Code is available at https://github.com/emehillaj/scalable-unrolled-mri.

title: LegoSR: A Unified Framework for Self-Improving Agent-Guided Scientific Discovery
abstract: Discovering equations from data provides governing laws, constitutive relations and closure models for scientific understanding and prediction. Yet a method that succeeds on one system may fail on another or on noisy data, so discovery depends on expert trial and error. Unsuccessful searches can still reveal useful parts of an equation, but these clues must be recognized and combined. We present LegoSR, a unified framework for agent-guided equation discovery built on composable discovery and cumulative experience. Seven complementary equation discovery methods and shared computational modules form reusable building blocks, connected through a common equation representation. Researchers can launch discovery with one command and guide it with partially known equations. LegoSR Agent selects methods, revises searches using feedback and combines partial findings into new hypotheses. Its Experience Library consolidates graded outcomes into lessons that guide later tasks across equation families. Evaluation covers 134 algebraic regression problems, 40 ordinary differential equation targets and 25 partial differential equation problems at several noise levels, together with three case studies. On noisy PDEs, LegoSR Agent recovers more equations than seven expert-tuned methods combined and stays close to them on ODEs. It also exceeds a generic agent with the same model, tools and budget by up to 28 percentage points, with 63-73% shorter median wall-clock time on PDE problems.

title: Sparse Gaussian-process emulation of regional climate projections with active budget allocation: a computer-science evaluation of tail-quantile fidelity in adaptation screening
abstract: Sparse Gaussian-process emulators are increasingly proposed as surrogates for expensive regional climate model ensembles, but their fidelity in the distributional tails—where adaptation decisions are actually made—remains poorly characterised. The framework is evaluated on NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Lagos, Nigeria (2000–2023, 312 observations), where the mean temperature was 26.414 °C and the warming trend was 0.1553 °C per decade. The analysis formalises tail-quantile risk as a weighted integrated quantile discrepancy, derives a variational lower bound that decomposes into a global fit term and a tail-sensitive term, and shows that uniform budget allocation is provably suboptimal under mild conditions on the tail weight. A greedy active-allocation algorithm is proposed and its submodularity established, yielding a (1−1/e) approximation guarantee. Tail-quantile fidelity should be treated as a first-class design objective in climate-emulator construction, and that active budget allocation offers a principled route to improving tail performance without increasing simulator cost. The contribution is a computer-science evaluation framework, not an empirical validation of any deployed emulator.

title: Embedding-Based Educational Taxonomies
abstract: Educational taxonomies organize educational content, such as exercise problems, into concepts, which are also called skills or knowledge components. These taxonomies define learning objectives in educational applications such as intelligent tutoring systems. Developed through human expertise and iterative refinement, they also provide fundamental structure for curricula, assessment, and models of student learning. Recent advances in semantic text embeddings make it possible to construct alternative educational taxonomies computationally from the content itself. In this paper, we investigate this possibility by clustering embeddings of math questions to construct embedding-based educational taxonomies. We compare these taxonomies with the existing Common Core State Standards (CCSS)-based knowledge-component taxonomies in two ASSISTments datasets and evaluate their utility in Deep Knowledge Tracing, a downstream task that relies on taxonomic mappings of questions to knowledge components. The embedding-based taxonomies exhibit substantial but incomplete correspondence with the existing taxonomies, revealing both preserved and alternative organizations of educational content. When used for knowledge tracing, they improve predictive performance by approximately 3-5 AUC percentage points. These results demonstrate the potential of semantic embeddings for automatically constructing educational taxonomies that both recover structure present in human-developed taxonomies and provide useful alternative representations for downstream educational modeling.

title: Propasafe-Hybrid: A Text-Based Hybrid Propaganda Detection Tool
abstract: Propagandistic content increasingly circulates through online news and social media, where readers often encounter it with limited scrutiny, highlighting the need for reliable and fine-grained detection. This paper introduces Propasafe-Hybrid, a sentence-level system that integrates a fine-tuned transformer classifier with LLM-based technique classification to identify, label, and explain specific propaganda strategies. The pipeline generates actionable outputs, including highlighted sentences, technique assignments, and concise rationales, so users can immediately understand why a sentence was flagged and how each label was determined. To control inference cost, Propasafe-Hybrid employs a cost-aware pre-filtering stage that forwards only high-likelihood sentences to LLMs, reducing token usage while preserving the underlying decision logic. Together, these design choices enhance the explainability, efficiency, and practical usability of sentence-level propaganda detection in real-world news environments.

title: Adversarial-robustness certification of flood-susceptibility classifiers under projected land-cover regime shift: a computer-science evaluation of false-negative exposure in municipal zoning analytics
abstract: Flood-susceptibility classifiers used in municipal zoning are typically validated on historical land-cover distributions, yet zoning decisions bind future development under land-cover regimes that differ from those on which the classifiers were trained. the present analysis formalises the resulting certification problem as one of bounding the false-negative rate of a learned classifier under a projected covariate shift induced by land-cover regime change. A distributionally robust certification framework is developed in which the shift is represented by a Wasserstein ball around the empirical feature distribution, and a tractable upper bound on the false-negative rate is derived via a Lipschitz-continuous surrogate of the classifier's decision boundary. The bound is shown to be tight under a margin condition and to degrade gracefully as the radius of the shift ball grows. A case study using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis air temperature for Harare, Zimbabwe (2000–2023, 312 monthly observations, mean 18.914 °C, warming trend 0.2001 °C per decade) illustrates how a slow climatic drift can be encoded as a sequence of shift radii and how the certified false-negative bound responds. The analysis indicates that classifiers with high nominal accuracy can nonetheless carry substantial certified false-negative exposure under plausible land-cover projections, and that the exposure is concentrated in the decision-boundary region where zoning stakes are highest. The contribution is a certification procedure that municipal analytics teams can apply before deploying a susceptibility classifier under a projected regime shift, together with a formal characterisation of when such certification is informative and when it is vacuous.

title: PathKGen: Pathology Knowledge Assisted MLLM for Explainable Histopathology
abstract: Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis serves as the fundamental method for the clinical diagnosis of cancer in digital histopathology. Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have enabled state-of-the-art (SOTA) automated histopathology report generation. However, MLLMs reason purely through distributions encoded in their neural parameters, limiting the amount of knowledge and reasoning logic they can contain given the model scale. Their black-box reasoning poses another challenge to the human interpretation of intermediate reasoning. We address these issues by utilizing knowledge graphs to inject external structured knowledge for MLLMs to reason over, while making this reasoning component visible. Knowledge graphs are capable of partially externalizing the containment of medical knowledge, an area that remains underexplored in pathology report generation. We introduce PathKGen, a knowledge graph-assisted MLLM for histopathology report generation. PathKGen has two main branches: (1) a visual path that learns visual token inputs to the MLLM using pathology foundation models, and (2) a knowledge path that learns knowledge token inputs by extracting key morphological features of WSIs through querying a pathology-specific knowledge graph. A comprehensive evaluation on WSI-Bench dataset shows that PathKGen surpasses previous SOTA methods while revealing diagnostic reasoning as visually intuitive graphs. Due to its modular design, the proposed knowledge path is complementary to vision-aligned MLLMs and can be extended to other applications by curating domain-specific knowledge graphs to generate knowledge tokens.

title: Semantic-First: Temporal Scheduling in Flow Matching for Reliable Emotional Image Generation
abstract: Affect-controlled image generation should change how a scene feels while preserving what the prompt specifies. We study the temporal allocation of stochastic exploration and policy optimization in flow-matching models as a means of controlling this balance. During RL training, our semantic-first schedule uses deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE) sampling during the high-noise phase and confines stochastic differential equation (SDE) exploration and group relative policy optimization (GRPO) to a late window. Controlled experiments separate exploration location, optimization location, and terminal-step sampling, showing distinct semantic benefits from late exploration and late updates. On FLUX.1-dev, semantic-first improves prompt faithfulness, independently evaluated affect accuracy, and human-rated semantic preservation and overall preference. The expanded semantic audit records 2.7% subject drift, while GRPO training time decreases by 41.1% relative to original full-path Flow-GRPO. Window-width experiments characterize the affect-semantic and computational trade-offs, and replication on SD3.5-Medium reproduces the scheduling advantage. These results establish denoising time as a practical control dimension for reliable emotional image generation.

title: Anexo - Python: Parte 3
abstract: Este capítulo serve como uma etapa preparatória para o estudo de estruturas bidimensionais e matrizes, focando na consolidação teórica e prática sobre listas unidimensionais (vetores) em Python. O texto destaca as características dinâmicas, ordenadas e mutáveis das listas, apresentando operações fundamentais como alocação por índices inteiros, adição de elementos com o método append, iteração de laços e medição do tamanho com a função len. Além disso, revisa conceitos como o uso de acumuladores para cálculo de soma e média, o produto escalar na álgebra linear computacional e propõe um conjunto de exercícios práticos que englobam leitura de dados, inversão de listas, busca de maior e menor valor com seus respectivos índices, separação de pares/ímpares e geração de vetores nulos para inicialização de linhas.

title: PACE: Research Proving Agent for Adaptive Conjecture Exploration
abstract: Many mathematical research agents focus on solving problems with fixed statements. However, conjecture research, especially in applied mathematics, may require revising candidate questions or conclusions as investigation proceeds, coupling problem formulation with proof development. We present PACE, a research-proof agent that supports this process through a structured research loop that selects mathematical objectives and develops or challenges candidate mechanisms. The whole prover constructs proofs from these mechanisms, and an independent verifier checks them against the original target. Evidence-tracking memory stores assumptions and dependencies arising during research and marks evidence for revalidation when a candidate or condition changes. This memory supports task-specific context composition that keeps checked premises, exploratory material and unresolved obligations distinct. To evaluate proof construction and conjecture research, we introduce ResearchProofBench, an applied-mathematics benchmark focused on optimization, comprising 51 known-proof tasks with 331 hidden checkpoints under historical abstract access and six open-problem cases. The known-proof tasks assess reconstruction of published results, while the open-problem cases assess mathematical investigation and proof development. On the 51 known-proof tasks, PACE achieves an aggregate Proof Score of 75.16 and completes 20 proofs. In conjecture research, PACE develops conditional results, with its submissions receiving higher review scores than the compared baselines.

title: FG-ConvNO: A Geometry-Aware Neural Operator for Propeller CFD Prediction
abstract: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is essential in contemporary engineering design, yet it remains expensive to compute and can take thousands of CPU/GPU hours or more for a single high-fidelity simulation. Recent developments in machine learning for scientific modeling have led to powerful surrogate frameworks that can approximate flow fields and physical quantities by using a fraction of the computational cost. However, most of these methods require largescale homogeneous datasets or simple geometries, exhibiting severe generalization gaps when applied to complex and data-scarce configurations. To address this, we propose the Factorized Geometry Convolutional Neural Operator (FG-ConvNO) for robust geometry-aware propeller pressure prediction under limited training data. We introduce geometryaware encoding, efficient interpolation-based decoding, and auxiliary global quantity supervision. In addition, we incorporate DISCO blocks that use discrete continuous convolutions to make the model discretization agnostic. In our experiments, FG-ConvNO achieves the highest accuracy for both surface pressure and global thrust prediction on a procedurally generated propeller CFD dataset. Geometry-aware encoding and architectural simplification improve stability, while random vertex subsampling enhances robustness. Overall, adding geometric priors to grid-based convolutional operators reduces overfitting on complex propeller geometries and improves generalization in low-data regimes.

title: Explainable hybrid ensemble framework for lung cancer classification using deep CNNs and random forest
abstract: Lung cancer is still a significant cause of cancer death in the world. Thoracic computed tomography (CT) classification can be helpful in earlier diagnosis and better patient management. However, many deep-learning techniques require large annotated datasets, large amounts of computational resources and the techniques are not easily interpretable. This manuscript introduces a comprehensible hybrid approach to multiclass lung cancer classification based on two different transfer-learning backbones, DenseNet169 and MobileNetV2. They used several ensemble techniques to combine their class-probability outputs. For qualitative visual explanations of the image regions contributing to each prediction, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) was applied to the image after inference. The framework was evaluated with two publicly available thoracic CT datasets that include both benign and malignant, normal and non-small-cell lung cancer categories. The accuracy of the Random Forest stacker for the Chest CT dataset was 99.50% and 99.54% for the IQ-OTH/NCCD dataset. The results show that DenseNet169 and MobileNetV2 complementary probability outputs could be used as an effective decision-fusion method in lung cancer classification from different datasets with different class structures and diagnostic categories. The Grad-CAM technique also made the model predictions more transparent by identifying image areas that influenced the prediction. In general, the proposed framework presents a practical and comprehensible method for automated lung cancer classification, and serves as a valuable guideline in future studies regarding the development of robust, explainable, and clinically relevant computer-aided diagnosis in medical imaging.

title: What Makes a Question Curious? Measuring Model Curiosity in Human-LLM Interactions
abstract: Large language models increasingly act as partners in everyday communication. In these interactions, useful assistance may require not only answering, but also asking the right questions that surface knowledge gaps, assumptions, and alternatives. In this study, we refer to such epistemic question-asking as model curiosity, and introduce a theory-grounded taxonomy that distinguishes curiosity-oriented questions from generic model questioning. Across four conversation datasets, we find that curiosity-oriented questions remain rare (17-28% of all questions), but are associated with more exploratory and epistemically rich subsequent user responses, with varying patterns across datasets. We further conduct a human study to evaluate the usefulness of model curiosity, finding that curiosity can encourage exploration, especially in advice, creative, and research contexts. title: Rescuing Your Pruning: Rethinking Visual Token Pruning and Post-Training Recovery in MLLMs
abstract: Visual token pruning substantially reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing methods are mostly training-free and plug-and-play. They treat the resulting performance drop as an inevitable cost of compression and pursue increasingly complex pruning rules. We rethink this view through two questions: how much of the loss can post-training rescue, and, building on this recovery, how can joint compression push pruning to its limit? We curate a 282K-sample post-training mixture covering general VQA, reasoning, OCR, and grounding, and post-train 36 configurations that drop or merge tokens under a unified protocol. Post-training rescues most of the loss, even for OCR and grounding, and its adaptation gain in closing the gap between the pruned and the dense model grows as the budget tightens. For joint compression, we find that the vision encoder, not the LLM, dominates prefill time in native-resolution MLLMs, so where tokens are removed matters more than how many: keeping 40% of tokens at the encoder runs faster than keeping 10% at the projector. Our best configuration prunes the encoder lightly and the projector aggressively, leaves the LLM intact, and keeps general understanding and reasoning at the dense level. It accelerates the LLM stage by 3.49x but the end-to-end time-to-first-token by only 1.54x, showing that LLM-stage speedups overstate end-to-end gains. We hope these findings offer insights for future research on joint visual token compression. Our data, protocol, and code will be released.

title: A Comprehensive Framework for All Stages of Large-Model Training: From Data and Tokenization, through Pretraining, to Post-Training Alignment
abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) arise from the synergy of the full training pipeline, including data and tokenization, pretraining, and post-training (supervised fine-tuning, preference alignment, reinforcement learning, and continual optimization), rather than any individual stage. Existing surveys mostly adopt a single-stage or single-technique perspective, treating related research as isolated systems without unified stage division or a horizontally comparable basis. This paper proposes a unified stage division and a six-dimensional analytical framework covering data, objective function, optimization strategy, system constraints, evaluation, and risk and governance. We systematically review 395 core references from 2017 to 2026, and present a conceptual map of cross-stage effects: forward constraints of pretraining on post-training, and reverse empowerment of post-training on data and pretraining. We derive three core findings. First, the comparability of scaling laws depends on data quality and mixture, a long-neglected variable. Second, preference alignment methods (RLHF, DPO) and reasoning reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards redefine post-training boundaries, while the Pass@1 versus Pass@K debate remains unresolved. Third, multimodal training poses structural challenges to the pure-text paradigm in tokenizer design, training objectives, and evaluation. The paper provides a cross-stage effects diagram, a method-family map, a practical decision tree, and at least 10 verifiable open problems, with an extensible skeleton for focused sub-surveys per stage. As of the retrieval date, peer-reviewed evidence (A+B) accounts for approximately 79% of the 395 references.

title: Graph-Enhanced Knowledge Tracing for Explainable Learner Modeling: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) has become a central approach for modeling students' evolving knowledge states, but conventional sequence-based KT models offer limited representation of relationships among skills, concepts, and assessment indicators, reducing their interpretability for monitoring mastery and learning progression. This study systematically reviews how graph-based and knowledge graph-enhanced KT models have been developed, integrated, and evaluated to support skill mastery, learning outcome monitoring, and assessment-related interpretation. A PRISMA-based Systematic Literature Review was conducted using Scopus and IEEE Xplore, covering publications indexed from 2015 to 2025. From 116 initial records, 20 studies satisfied the eligibility criteria for active graph-enhanced KT and were included in the synthesis corpus, comprising 8 core (40.0%) and 12 supporting (60.0%) studies. Six major integration families were identified, including GCN/GNN-based, Knowledge Graph/ontology-enhanced, heterogeneous or multiplex graph, attention-over-graph, Q-matrix/concept map-based KT, and graph-supported recommendation. Graph-enhanced KT can enrich learner-state representation, support skill and mastery interpretation, and strengthen explainable learner modeling, particularly among core studies. However, active graph-KT integration remains limited, and issues of construct validity, cross-domain generalization, fairness, and deployment-oriented evaluation remain underexplored.

title: Why Does Structured Output Fail? An Empirical Study of Prompt-Enforced Pydantic Schemas Across Nine LLMs
abstract: Pipelines that require structured outputs from hosted language models often specify a Pydantic schema in the prompt, validate the response, and retry when validation fails. Although native structured-output modes provide an alternative, application-side validation remains important for enforcing custom constraints. Yet pipeline reliability is often summarized by a single validity rate, which obscures why outputs fail and which interventions may help. We introduce a fine-grained taxonomy of schema-conformance failures and a deterministic classifier that assigns failure categories from model responses and Pydantic validation errors. We apply this framework to 3,997 generation attempts across nine OpenAI and Anthropic model/API configurations, using questions from HotpotQA and FinanceBench. Our results show that similar validity rates can mask different failure patterns, and that dominant failure categories vary with schema constraints and task. Markdown-fenced JSON is the most common failure: among 681 fenced failures, only 48.0% pass validation after fence removal, while the remainder conceal additional violations, predominantly field-length violations. In an exploratory prompt ablation, variants that suppress fences appear to shift failures toward length violations, but the shift is consistent with exposing violations that were already present, illustrating how aggregate validity rates can obscure changes in failure composition. We derive four engineering practices for validator, schema, retry and evaluation design, three supported by our data and one, on retry feedback, proposed but not tested, and release the classifier, completions, and annotations.

title: EXE: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Pretraining via Factorized Latent Actions for VLA Models
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are bottlenecked by the scarcity of robot data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer an abundant, diverse, and semantically-rich alternative that inherently captures manipulation intent. However, the embodiment gap makes it difficult to extract action-relevant representations from these videos. From the perspective of action execution, human hands and robots share analogous manipulation primitives---reaching, grasping, placing---yet exhibit distinct kinematics tied to their embodiments. This might motivate our key approach: egocentric video pretraining can yield shared action representations capturing transferable manipulation skills, while human-specific motion patterns should be disentangled to avoid interfering with robot policy learning. To this end, we propose EXE, an Egocentric Cross(X)-Embodiment pretraining framework that learns a factorized latent action representation from egocentric human videos, separating shared manipulation priors from embodiment-specific signals. By leveraging the shared action space, the robot policy acquires generalizable manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations without being biased by human-specific kinematics. This shared knowledge transfers across embodiments with different kinematic structures, enabling the same pretraining to benefit both parallel grippers and dexterous hands. EXE yields consistent gains over baseline without pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.

title: BoardSafety: AI-Ready Data from Manufacturer Documentation for Development-Board Safety
abstract: The development of large language models (LLMs) are capable to assist with hardware experiments. In this scenario, this raises a practical question: Can LLMs determine whether a proposed operation is safe for a specific development board? Documented operating limits and safety requirements are board-specific, even across products from the same manufacturer. This variation makes board-specific safety judgments by an LLM difficult to evaluate. To address this problem, we introduce the BoardSafety Benchmark. The benchmark is built from vendor datasheets and hardware guides. For data transformation, these documents are converted into a board-specific safety rule base and are then used to create labeled operating scenarios. Each data item pairs a board and a proposed operation to an applicable safety rule with ground-truth label, indicating the level of safety. The categorized level for each operation includes safe, unsafe, or insufficient-info. In addition, the benchmark covers diverse operations, board-specific cases, boundary conditions, and missing-information cases. We evaluate a series of models by varying their access to board-specific rules and the use of structured-rationale prompting. Our results demonstrate that providing the safety rules generally improves accuracy, whereas structured-rationale prompting produces gains that vary across models and rule-access conditions. Overall, the evaluated models cannot yet reliably determine whether an operation is safe, which implies that critical exploration is required for this field.

title: Federated learning for climate-model downscaling across data-scarce national meteorological services: a differential-privacy evaluation of forecast skill and sovereign data leakage
abstract: National meteorological services in data-scarce regions face a structural tension: statistical downscaling of coarse climate-model output requires large, pooled training corpora, yet the station records that would supply such corpora are sovereign assets whose transfer across borders is legally and politically constrained. Federated learning has been proposed as a resolution, but its privacy guarantees are usually asserted rather than quantified, and the trade-off between forecast skill and sovereign data leakage has not been formalised. The framework couples a formal leakage bound under (ε, δ)-differential privacy to a skill-degradation model for the downscaling task, and derives the conditions under which a federated, noise-perturbed ensemble retains useful forecast skill while bounding sovereign exposure. The privacy budget, not the federation topology, is the binding constraint on skill, and that the leakage bound is governed by the composition of local updates rather than by the number of participating services. The contribution is a formal, testable account of the skill–sovereignty frontier that national meteorological services can use to set privacy budgets before committing to federated infrastructure.

title: Schema-Free Text-to-SQL: Learning Enterprise Database Structure from Query Logs
abstract: Text-to-SQL systems achieve remarkable accuracy on academic benchmarks, yet performance drops dramatically in enterprise deployments. This gap stems from a fundamental assumption: existing approaches require complete schema documentation, but enterprise databases typically lack comprehensive documentation, featuring cryptic naming and implicit relationships. We present the first text-to-SQL framework that operates without schema documentation, instead learning database structure from historical query logs. Query logs encode implicit structural knowledge: which tables are queried together, how they join, and what columns map to business concepts. We construct a knowledge graph from parsed query patterns and introduce entity-driven GraphRAG retrieval that grounds user questions in domain terminology rather than relying solely on embedding similarity. Validated on both an industrial deployment with expert evaluation and the Beaver benchmark, our approach substantially outperforms similarity-based retrieval methods, the dominant industry approach, in both executability and answer quality. On Beaver, we achieve 95.7% execution validity compared to 60.8% for embedding-based retrieval, with expert data engineers preferring our system 70% to 10% on internal deployment. Our work demonstrates that text-to-SQL can operate effectively in schema-ambiguous enterprise environments, enabling natural language database interfaces "in the wild".

title: More: Mode-Optimized Reasoning with Self-Adaptive Effort for Self-Evolving Agents
abstract: Self-evolving training improves the performance of agents on difficult tasks through verifiable feedback, but it often applies costly deliberation uniformly across tasks. To address this problem, we propose Mode-Optimized Reasoning with Self-Adaptive Effort (MORE), a self-evolving training framework that adaptively selects both reasoning form and computational effort for each task. Specifically, MORE follows a two-stage training paradigm: (i) \emph{Stage 1} establishes a compact prior over direct answering, short and long chain-of-thought, and code-based reasoning, and (ii) \emph{Stage 2} self-evolves this prior with Mode-Adaptive and Test-time Effort PPO (MATE-PPO) on generated, verifiable task streams without curated data. By learning mode selection and token expenditure jointly, MORE allocates concise reasoning to tasks that permit it while retaining extended deliberation where it is useful. Across coding, mathematics, and general-reasoning benchmarks, MORE achieves consistent performance gains on Base and Coder backbones at model scales from 3B to 14B. During inference, MORE demonstrates higher accuracy and better efficiency, with markedly shorter response lengths and reduced inference time.

title: From Intelligence to Autonomy: Foundations and Construction of Autonomous Agents for Future Intelligent Systems
abstract: Artificial intelligence is moving from one-off perception and generation tasks toward long-term planning, tool use, and interaction with real environments. Greater task competence, however, does not automatically yield autonomy: an external actor may still have to set goals, sustain operating conditions, detect failures, and approve updates. We define an autonomous agent as a system that, within explicit identity and authority boundaries, maintains both task goals and viability conditions, acts continuously using models of the world and itself, and adjusts its control mechanisms and long-term capabilities through feedback. We trace the conceptual path from homeostasis and feedback control to autopoiesis and biological autonomy. We then distinguish six lines of operationalization: computational autopoiesis, behavior-based robotics, agent formalization, adaptive software, embodied adaptation, and robotic self-modeling. On this basis, we propose a one-boundary, four-loop framework in which Operational, Viability, Reflexive, and Learning loops organize task execution, self-maintenance, metacontrol, and governed learning. Five paired simulation experiments test permission constraints, road-closure response, health maintenance, capability re-estimation, and cross-task learning. Their results provide preliminary evidence for the feasibility of these mechanisms, while broader environments and physical systems remain to be tested.

title: Differentially private computed generation of household energy-consumption microdata for urban heat-vulnerability mapping: a computer-science evaluation of equity-audit distortion under DP budgets
abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly proposed as the mechanism by which household energy microdata can be released for climate-analytics applications such as urban heat-vulnerability mapping, yet the distortion that DP noise introduces into equity audits of those data has not been characterised formally. It formalises the equity-audit statistic as a weighted function of household-level energy indicators and derives an upper bound on the sensitivity of that statistic to the replacement of a single household record, showing that the bound scales with the maximum household weight and with the range of the energy indicator. The bound is then propagated through the Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms to obtain closed-form expressions for the noise scale required to achieve a target (ε, δ)-guarantee, and the resulting mean-squared distortion of the audit statistic is expressed as a function of ε, the number of households, and the weight concentration. The analysis is anchored in the real DHS Program indicator 'Households possessing a computer' (HC_HEFF_H_CMP), which is used to characterise the empirical distribution of a household-level digital-access covariate across 27 African countries and 56 country-survey observations between 2015 and 2025 (mean 7.893, standard deviation 5.144, minimum Guinea 1.50, maximum South Africa 22.00).

title: TurboWAM: Learning What Matters for Fast World Action Models
abstract: World action models have demonstrated promising performance in robot policy learning, yet their high inference latency remains a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment. Recent approaches have sought to improve inference efficiency by eliminating test-time future-frame imagination or accelerating action prediction. However, aggregating representations from all video world model layers can introduce redundant computation, while standard backpropagation may distribute action-supervision gradients unevenly across layers, limiting the effectiveness of world representation learning. In this work, we propose TurboWAM, a fast world action model that learns to efficiently aggregate and optimize world representations for action prediction. Specifically, TurboWAM introduces an efficient world representation aggregation mechanism that restricts aggregation to a bounded range of relevant world model layers identified through layer relevance analysis. Within this bounded range, TurboWAM estimates aggregation weights for different world model layers based on the current action denoising state and combines them with learnable layer-wise weights to fuse world representations. Moreover, TurboWAM employs a world model gradient modulation mechanism that decomposes action-supervision gradients into a layer-shared component and layer-specific residual components, enabling more balanced gradient propagation across world model layers. This mechanism operates exclusively during training and introduces no additional inference computation. Together, these designs enable more efficient world representation learning and low-latency action prediction. Extensive experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks show that TurboWAM achieves low inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates compared with state-of-the-art methods.

Moreover, TurboWAM employs a world model gradient modulation mechanism that decomposes action-supervision gradients into a layer-shared component and layer-specific residual components, enabling more balanced gradient propagation across world model layers. This mechanism operates exclusively during training and introduces no additional inference computation. Together, these designs enable more efficient world representation learning and low-latency action prediction. Extensive experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks show that TurboWAM achieves low inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates compared with state-of-the-art methods.

title: Meta-CLIP: Metadata-Conditioned Contrastive Learning for Zero-Shot Disease Inference
abstract: Medical vision--language pretraining learns transferable representations from paired images and radiology reports, yet differences in scanners and acquisition protocols can impair transfer. Existing approaches primarily enrich clinical semantics, leaving structured acquisition information in DICOM headers underused. We introduce Meta-CLIP, a metadata-conditioned contrastive framework that uses acquisition similarity to reweight cross-modal negatives during pretraining. A kernel over numerical and categorical DICOM fields defines a bounded pairwise margin. This margin increases the contribution of acquisition-similar negatives, emphasizing distinctions among studies that share imaging conditions. The kernel remains fixed during image--text optimization, and inference follows the standard dual-encoder architecture without requiring metadata. We evaluate Meta-CLIP on chest radiography and volumetric chest CT through zero-shot classification, appearance perturbations, grounding, and representation analyses. On CT-RATE, Meta-CLIP improves macro-AUROC over CT-CLIP by 1.41 points, with a 95\% paired bootstrap confidence interval of 0.96--1.85 points. It also achieves the highest macro-AUROC on four of five CXR benchmarks. An exploratory BrgSA evaluation extends the analysis to another CT backbone. These findings support acquisition metadata as a practical training-time prior for medical vision--language learning. Code will be made publicly available upon publication.

title: Adaptive Transfer of Representational Signatures for LLM Reliability Detection
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are reported to be susceptible to reliability issues including hallucinations and reasoning errors. Existing quality detectors can predict unreliable outputs based on internal representations with decent accuracies. However, training these detectors often requires substantial domain-specific labeled data, which limits their applicability to new domains. We propose to address this challenge by transferring representational signatures across related domains. More specifically, we build a statistical framework that first extracts low-dimensional signatures for each domain, then uses cross-fitting to learn composition weights of domain-specific predictors. The weights adapt to each source domain's predictive relevance to the target domain. Our asymptotic analysis of a least-squares analogue characterizes the limiting prediction risk and aggregation weights in terms of domain discrepancies and representation bias. Experiments across multiple hallucination datasets and open-weight LLMs show that, with only 25 labeled questions in the new domain, adaptive transfer improves hallucination-detection AUROC by 6.8%. For reasoning-step prediction, it improves AUROC by 8.4%.

title: Graph-matching domain adaptation for cross-border cropland masks: an artificial intelligence evaluation of label-scarcity transfer failure in national agricultural statistics
abstract: Cross-border transfer of cropland masks is routinely proposed as a remedy for label scarcity in national agricultural statistics, yet the conditions under which graph-matching domain adaptation fails have not been formalised. The analysis treats label scarcity as a structural property of the target domain rather than a sampling deficiency, and derives a bound on target risk that separates three additive components: graph-matching distortion, label-scarcity variance, and the divergence between source and target cropland definitions. The bound is used to identify a transfer-failure threshold below which adaptation is dominated by the unadapted source classifier. A formal proposition establishes that graph-matching distortion grows with the spectral gap between source and target adjacency structures, and a corollary shows that this distortion is not reduced by increasing the number of unlabelled target samples. The paper does not report empirical estimates; it provides the formal apparatus, the failure criterion, and the diagnostic quantities that a national statistical office would need to compute before adopting a transferred mask. The contribution is a specification of when cross-border graph-matching adaptation should be rejected, and a set of computable indicators that make that rejection auditable.

title: Stable and Calibrated Latent Force ODE Filters
abstract: Estimating unobserved forces in mechanistic systems is a central task of scientific machine learning. Approximate Gaussian filtering methods that synthesize mechanistic and empirical information have shown remarkable capacity in jointly identifying latent processes together with the system state in a single forward-backward pass. The resulting latent force ODE filter framework channels information from observational data specifically into the unknown parts of the system. This work addresses open questions about calibration and stability of the method. We show that the joint posterior over state and force is the reweighted conventional latent force posterior. This uncovers a crucial dependence of the stability of the method on the prior variance of the system state, which effectively controls the flow of information from observations to the latent force through the mechanistic system. From this insight, we construct an improved algorithm that provides stable and calibrated plug-and-play inference. We demonstrate the improved framework on several simulated experimental settings.

title: Extraction meets Distillation - cryptanalytic techniques to recover parameters from a Deep Neural Network
abstract: We study fully connected neural-network reconstruction by combining cryptanalytic weight-direction extraction with learning from predicted labels. We adapt a ReLU extraction implementation to Leaky ReLU, compare sign-search methods, and estimate biases and output layers. We prove conditional bounds for direction recovery with approximate prefixes, preservation of local distance votes, prediction changes from aligned parameter errors, and sign selection with independent scoring data. We also specify exact row restoration and distinguish its guarantee from that of gradient masking. The experiments evaluate assisted extraction, with privileged access to gradients, hidden activations, and victim parameters, followed by label-based reconstruction. Across eight search seeds on the largest synthetic architecture, Leaky ReLU recovers 51--57 neurons in the deepest hidden layer, while ReLU recovers none. This advantage does not hold uniformly across architectures and layers. Removing victim-weight access from the sign walk gives less accurate signs, despite high final prediction agreement. Across 40 seeded runs on the two smallest synthetic victims, agreement on 5,000 inputs excluded from fitting and selection ranges from $0.9890$ to $0.9992$. On two CIFAR-10 victims, the reconstructed models achieve $56.40\%$ and $58.29\%$ agreement and exceed the distillation baseline on three functional metrics. We report label requests separately from privileged access and explain why prediction agreement does not identify network parameters.

title: Quantifying Meaning with SCAPE-T: Semantic Complexity from Encoder-Only Transformer Attention
abstract: Automated semantic complexity estimation remains underexplored in NLP, despite important applications in linguistics and interpretability. This paper defines semantic complexity as the code length required to uniquely specify a text's semantic meaning, and operationalises it via SCAPE-T, an attention-derived metric based on encoder-only transformers. Existing measures either model reader effort (readability, lexical difficulty), which correlates with surface features (word length, syntax), or quantify surface features directly (type-token ratio, word frequency). SCAPE-T targets semantic integration directly by combining three submetrics: (i) inverse-weighted self-focus (token-to-self), (ii) CLS focus (token-to-CLS), and (iii) inter-head redundancy (cosine similarity across heads), using layer-weighted aggregation; data-driven learning is confined to hyperparameter tuning for calibration. Development uses philosophical prose vs. MCTest stories; evaluation is on children's stories vs. technical Wikipedia articles, with pairwise accuracy on contrasts as the primary criterion. Baselines include readability, syntactic/lexical, and LLM-derived measures. SCAPE-T substantially outperforms all tested baselines under word-length control, with a pairwise accuracy of 78.5% (95% bootstrap CI: 76.1-80.4, N=10k pairwise comparisons; +12.7 percentage points over the strongest baseline); without that control, readability heuristics overtake, consistent with their reliance on surface features. On a short-terms abstractness dataset, SCAPE-T also leads. Ablations show each submetric contributes materially. Overall, the results show SCAPE-T isolates conceptual structure from lexical/syntactic confounds better than existing methods, and generalises across two held-out domains.

title: Multi-scale LSTM forecasting with attention-based feature fusion for anomaly detection in multivariate monitoring data
abstract: Abstract Engineering systems such as power equipment and industrial processes are monitored through multivariate time series whose anomalies appear at different temporal scales, from short fluctuations to deviations that persist over a whole operating cycle. A detector that reads a single input window has to commit to one of these scales. This paper presents MAF-LSTM, a forecasting-based anomaly detection framework in which parallel long short-term memory (LSTM) branches read input windows of different lengths, a scale-level attention module fuses their representations into a one-step-ahead forecast, and the forecasting residuals are scored with the Mahalanobis distance estimated on normal validation data. Experiments on smart meter data, two sets of high-voltage converter modulator pulses and a simulated chemical process show that MAF-LSTM achieves the highest AU-ROC and AU-PR of the five compared methods on all four datasets, exceeding the best baseline by 3.20 and 5.33 percentage points on average. An ablation study on the smart meter data quantifies the contribution of each component and shows that multi-scale modeling is most beneficial for anomalies with pronounced within-day fluctuation, where it matches or exceeds the best single-window model on each anomaly type without requiring the window length to be tuned.

title: HerHealthGPT: An Evidence-Grounded Conversational AI System for Women's Reproductive Health
abstract: "Why is my period late?" Sometimes, the most useful response begins with another question. Yet conversational AI systems may respond to incomplete health queries without seeking essential context or grounding their guidance in verifiable evidence. This paper introduces HerHealthGPT, an evidence-grounded conversational AI system designed to address these challenges in women's reproductive health. HerHealthGPT integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), context-aware clarification, and source validation within an interactive web interface. Rather than responding immediately to incomplete queries, the system maintains conversational context, asks targeted follow-up questions, checks for premature conclusions, and grounds its responses in retrieved evidence. We evaluate the AI components using 540 English messages derived from 90 reproductive-health cases and conduct a prototype questionnaire study with 30 adults. Evidence retrieval improves concern-category accuracy from 54.1% to 59.3% compared with fine-tuning alone. The clarification router achieves 85.6% recall and 86.2% specificity on constructed targets. In the user study, 83.3% of participants preferred the retrieval-enabled configuration, while 25 of 30 considered its follow-up questions relevant. These findings suggest that integrating evidence retrieval with interactive clarification offers a promising approach to more transparent, context-aware reproductive-health information systems, while further clinical validation remains necessary.

title: Beyond Affine Reconstruction: Multi-Resolution Transformer DeepONets for the Radiative Transfer Equation
abstract: Radiative heat transfer plays a dominant role in fire simulations, where solving the radiative transfer equation (RTE) is a computational bottleneck. Neural operators can accelerate these computations by learning solution operators from offline simulation data. However, conventional DeepONet surrogates rely on fixed-grid inputs and affine reconstruction, limiting their flexibility across resolutions and their approximation accuracy at a fixed latent dimension. In this paper, we develop a transformer-based DeepONet for multi-resolution RTE surrogate modelling. The proposed approach combines a Perceiver encoder, which maps temperature and absorption coefficient fields at different spatial resolutions into a fixed-size latent representation, with a cross-attention decoder that enables non-affine reconstruction of the radiative intensity. This architecture allows a single model to process inputs at varying resolutions without resampling them onto a common grid. We formulate a computable empirical version of a previously derived theoretical lower bound for affine reconstruction, enabling direct comparison with model errors on the same dataset. Experiments on a two-dimensional pool-fire dataset demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms autoencoder-based DeepONets in predicting both radiative intensity and incident radiation, with fewer trainable parameters. Power spectral density analysis shows improved preservation of small-scale structures. Both affine baselines remain above the corresponding lower bound at all evaluated ranks, whereas the proposed model achieves a training error below it at one matched latent dimension, demonstrating the potential of non-affine reconstruction to overcome this representational limitation. Experiments on a dataset combining three spatial resolutions confirm the accuracy advantage of the approach at each input resolution.

title: Perturbation-Based Data Selection for Medical Question Answering
abstract: Selecting a compact training subset is an important step in adapting medical language models from existing question-answering banks. We investigate perturbation-based data selection using two signals derived from Gaussian perturbations of the final-block representation: prediction-change frequency and non-flipping margin contraction. After a shared entropy prefilter, Representation-Sensitivity Prioritization (RSP) combines the signals using automatic root-mean-square scaling, while RSP-Drop ranks candidates by contraction alone. Both selectors use only questions and answer options during selection. We evaluate them with MedGemma-4B on five medical QA datasets at retained-set budgets of 64, 128, and 256 examples. At the primary budget of 128, RSP and RSP-Drop obtain dataset-averaged Macro-F1 scores of 47.55 and 48.28, respectively, compared with 45.11 for entropy-pool-matched random selection. Their relative performance varies across datasets and budgets. A selected-set case study identifies contrasting clean-margin profiles among the examples exchanged by the two rules, while a full-pool ablation shows that entropy prefiltering is not uniformly beneficial. These retrospective results characterize the empirical utility and limitations of perturbation-based selection under a fixed adaptation protocol. Evaluation uses one backbone and benchmarks with documented training-family overlap; it does not establish clinical effectiveness.

title: Effects of Adversarial Training of Word Embeddings on Chinese Agricultural Pest and Disease Named Entity Recognition with BERT-CRF
abstract: Entity boundaries, confusable entity types and surface forms absent from the training data all make it harder to extract structured information from agricultural pest and disease texts. We examined whether single-step adversarial training of word embeddings with the fast gradient method (FGM) improves entity recognition when the BERT-CRF inference architecture is left unchanged. On the official 13-type AgCNER corpus, with exact matching of character span and entity type, we compared a feature-based CRF, BiLSTM-CRF, BERT-CRF and BERT-CRF+FGM, training each neural model with three fixed random seeds. BERT-CRF+FGM reached mean test precision, recall and F1 of 94.37%, 95.10% and 94.73%. Its F1 was 0.28 percentage points higher than that of the matched BERT-CRF baseline, and the paired difference was positive for every seed. F1 on unseen surface forms rose from 74.87% to 76.41%, and the overall gain remained 0.27 percentage points after test texts duplicated in other splits were removed. Mean F1 increased for 11 of the 13 types but fell for Company and Organization. FGM did not change the parameter count. The seed-42 model produced 20,670 indexed entity occurrences that can be checked against the released records and character spans. The official test set had been used in an earlier baseline study and test results informed model adoption, so these findings are exploratory; independently sourced data are needed to assess how far they generalize.

title: EnerGNN: Learning Optimization-Compatible Energy Functions for Exact Constrained Combinatorial Inference
abstract: Learning-based approaches to combinatorial optimization often predict solutions directly or use predictions to restrict search, while expressive energy-based models typically rely on approximate inference. We introduce EnerGNN, a framework that learns energy functions over complete binary configurations and minimizes them under explicit hard constraints through mixed integer programming (MIP). EnerGNN combines a graph neural network encoder with an optimization-compatible readout and a nonlinear energy head, enabling exact constrained inference over the learned energy. An optimality-aware contrastive loss trains the energy to reflect solution quality and constraint violations. Across Quadratic Knapsack, Combinatorial Auctions, and a personalized cell therapy supply chain problem, EnerGNN achieves near-optimal solutions with 100% feasibility. On the supply chain problem, it achieves a 0.05% mean primal gap and a 17.4$\times$ speedup over the monolithic MIP. The learned energy also generalizes to larger instances and supports zero-shot constraint injection, adapting to changing constraints without retraining while preserving feasibility.

title: SWE-Ladder: Learning to Localize, Reproduce, and Patch via Progressive Privileged Self-Distillation
abstract: Resolving a repository-level issue typically requires a software-engineering (SWE) agent to localize the faulty code, reproduce the failure, and patch the code. Reinforcement learning trains such agents from a single test result on the final patch, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) adds token-level supervision from a teacher with privileged evidence, exposing the full reference patch at every step. Neither provides stage-specific guidance for localization or reproduction. We propose SWE-Ladder, which turns the verified repair of each training instance into stage-specific evidence: the changed files and lines for localization, the fail-to-pass tests for reproduction, and the diff for patching. A rule-based router assigns each step of an end-to-end rollout to a stage based on its tool call, a frozen teacher sees only the matching evidence, and the stages are distilled in repair order while GRPO optimizes the full trajectory. With Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on SWE-bench Verified under the R2E-Gym scaffold, SWE-Ladder improves pass@1 from 9.6% to 16.4%, compared with 10.4% for GRPO and 12.4% for OPSD with the full patch. Under the OpenHands scaffold, it improves pass@1 from 13.0% to 17.6%. Reversing the stage order under R2E-Gym reduces pass@1 to 11.4%.

evidence.title: SWE-Ladder: Learning to Localize, Reproduce, and Patch via Progressive Privileged Self-Distillation
evidence.abstract: Resolving a repository-level issue typically requires a software-engineering (SWE) agent to localize the faulty code, reproduce the failure, and patch the code. Reinforcement learning trains such agents from a single test result on the final patch, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) adds token-level supervision from a teacher with privileged evidence, exposing the full reference patch at every step. Neither provides stage-specific guidance for localization or reproduction. We propose SWE-Ladder, which turns the verified repair of each training instance into stage-specific evidence: the changed files and lines for localization, the fail-to-pass tests for reproduction, and the diff for patching. A rule-based router assigns each step of an end-to-end rollout to a stage based on its tool call, a frozen teacher sees only the matching evidence, and the stages are distilled in repair order while GRPO optimizes the full trajectory. With Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on SWE-bench Verified under the R2E-Gym scaffold, SWE-Ladder improves pass@1 from 9.6% to 16.4%, compared with 10.4% for GRPO and 12.4% for OPSD with the full patch. Under the OpenHands scaffold, it improves pass@1 from 13.0% to 17.6%. Reversing the stage order under R2E-Gym reduces pass@1 to 11.4%.

title: Combinatorial Lock for Trojan-Resilient AI Engines via Hash-Assisted Spectral Filtering
abstract: Multi-trigger backdoor attacks, in which heterogeneous trigger mechanisms (e.g., patch, blend, warping, and the latent-domain Spy-Watermark) coexist within a single poisoned model, cannot be addressed by existing shortcut-based defenses that assume a single, static attack mechanism. Current multi-trigger remedies (BU+FT, BU+ANP, and BU+ABL) rely on backdoor unlearning, which incurs high training costs and loses effectiveness at low poisoning ratios. This paper proposes Combinatorial Lock, a training-free, reference-calibrated defense that reduces multi-trigger identification to a combinatorial problem over binary activation signatures. This formulation is the key novelty: it yields a multi-trigger defense that is training-free, trigger-oblivious, and directly implementable in hardware, since its decision rules can be evaluated with integer and logic operations. The framework combines anomaly-gated spectral scrubbing, which removes the malicious subspace only from inputs identified as anomalous, with a hash-compressed combinatorial signature verified by an ensemble of detection experts, including a compound-attack-aware expert for multi-trigger inputs. A joint threshold-shrinkage search identifies an operating point ($τ$ at the 97.1st percentile, $γ= 0.78$) that reduces the attack success rate (ASR) to as low as 0.1% while preserving 97.8% clean accuracy. Evaluation on six models (ResNet18, VGG16, MobileNet, AlexNet, ViT-Small, ViT-Base) shows strong generalization: near-100% ASR drops to single digits across poisoning rates of 1-10% and 1-9 simultaneous triggers, with only gradual degradation in clean accuracy. ASIC and FPGA implementations confirm practicality, adding a consistent 19-20% latency overhead across all evaluated architectures and establishing Combinatorial Lock as a hardware-native approach to multi-trigger backdoor mitigation.

title: Federated learning of crop-disease classifiers across quarantine-silenced phytosanitary archives: a computer-science evaluation of privacy-utility trade-offs for cross-border outbreak analytics
abstract: Phytosanitary archives hold the labelled crop-disease observations that cross-border outbreak analytics require, yet quarantine regulation, commercial confidentiality and national data sovereignty keep those archives closed to centralised training. the present analysis formalises federated learning over such archives as a constrained optimisation problem in which each participating authority trains a local classifier on its own held-out data and shares only parameter updates under a differential-privacy mechanism. The framework is evaluated analytically rather than empirically: we derive a Rényi-differential-privacy accountant for the interleaved Gaussian mechanism, bound the generalisation gap of the federated averaged classifier as a function of archive heterogeneity and privacy budget, and characterise the privacy-utility frontier as a Pareto surface whose curvature is governed by the number of participating archives and the Dirichlet concentration of their label distributions. The analysis is illustrated with a reanalysis of NASA POWER MERRA-2 monthly air temperature for Kampala, Uganda (0.35° N, 32.58° E), 2000–2023, comprising 312 monthly observations with a mean of 22.443 °C and a linear warming trend of −0.1564 °C per decade, used here only to fix the climatic covariate distribution under which the classifier operates. The contribution is a decision procedure that lets a regional plant-protection organisation choose a privacy budget, an archive-participation set and a communication round count that together meet a stated outbreak-detection utility target without centralising any raw observation.

title: WebViSE: Scaling Visual Design Intelligence from the Open Web for LLM Website Generation
abstract: Large language models have made remarkable strides in website development, enabling complete and interactive web experiences to be built from natural-language instructions with far less effort. Yet, non-expert users often struggle to articulate sophisticated visual and interaction designs in natural language. Meanwhile, the open web already contains a vast reservoir of such design knowledge, embodied in mature website implementations. To this end, we introduce Website-derived Visual Skill Extraction (WebViSE), a framework that automatically abstracts these implementations into reusable Visual Skills and builds a structured Skill library. To scale the library, WebViSE organizes its Skills in a multi-parent DAG and jointly evolves Skill descriptions and DAG structure using Skill-conditioned Potential Queries, enabling efficient matching between diverse user instructions and relevant Skills. The auto-evolved structure outperforms non-hierarchical LLM retrieval baselines at only 39.09% of the estimated retrieval cost with Qwen3.8-Max. For any models, WebViSE can be directly injected as plug-and-play guidance, enabling diverse models to produce more visually compelling and aesthetically refined web pages. For open-source models, WebViSE can be used to build a data-synthesis pipeline that internalizes visual design intelligence into model weights. Experiments across multiple web development benchmarks and human evaluation consistently show that WebViSE improves the visual quality and interaction fidelity of artifacts. Overall, our work establishes an automated path for extracting, organizing, and transferring design intelligence from the open web to website-building models. We release all extracted Visual Skills, the associated Skill DAG, and our code at https://github.com/YifeiSun-0710/WebViSE.

title: Tracking Is Not Sensing: Artifact-Aware Thermal Video Respiration Estimation in Head-Free Marmosets
abstract: Continuous physiological monitoring is essential for linking behavior, internal state, and neural activity in neuroscience and translational research. In common marmosets, a key nonhuman primate model for social neuroscience, respiratory rate provides a basic readout of arousal, stress, and physiological regulation. Contact sensors can provide accurate measurements, but they add preparation burden and may interfere with head-free behavioral protocols. Thermal video offers a noncontact alternative by capturing breathing-related temperature changes around the nose and mouth. However, in head-free marmosets, these cues are weak, localized, and easily corrupted by head motion, pose changes, and fur. Here we show that this setting exposes a broader challenge in video-based physiological sensing: visually reliable tracking does not necessarily imply physiologically valid measurement. Using synchronized thermal video and contact respiration recordings, we show that marmoset respiration is recoverable from thermal video but strongly ROI-sensitive. Under head-free motion, visually plausible nasal tracking can still produce traces inconsistent with contact respiration, demonstrating that tracking is not sensing. We therefore estimate respiratory rate from learned temporal signals extracted from thermal clips and introduce Selective Temporal Attenuation Regularization (STAR). STAR selectively attenuates high-motion thermal discontinuities through local temporal imputation during training, regularizing models toward respiration-consistent dynamics while leaving inference unchanged on raw video. Across multiple deep-learning backbones, STAR improves head-free estimation, reaching 2.23 bpm MAE compared with 20.76 bpm for tracked ROI analysis.

title: Examining form-based linguistic productivity in people and large language models
abstract: Linguistic productivity, as evidenced by the use of words in novel contexts, is one of the most striking facts about human language. However, how abstract the knowledge that enables such productivity is remains unclear. We compare people's and computational language models' linguistic productivity in contexts where successful generalization depends on form-based information. We focus on extending the use of a novel verb learned in the active voice to passive contexts. We find people extend active to passive uses in a way consistent with abstract generalizations concerning linguistic form, even when no plausible meaning can be assigned to the novel verb. In contrast, large language models succeeded only when a meaning like an existing verb's could be assigned to the novel verb. We conclude that computational models' syntactic knowledge remains tied to the distribution and meaning of specific lexical items in a way that human syntactic knowledge is not.
